questions.question: How does World War II context affect "An Inspector Calls"?
questions.correctAnswer: WWII context means the audience has experienced catastrophe. They know what Birling doesn't - that war is coming. The play argues that pre-war attitudes (selfishness, inequality) led to disaster and must change.

questions.question: Why did Priestley set his play in 1912?
questions.correctAnswer: Setting in 1912 creates dramatic irony. The Birlings don't know about the wars, the Titanic sinking, the Russian Revolution. Their confidence in progress and stability is shown to be wrong. Priestley critiques the past from a knowing present.

questions.question: What does the Inspector represent in terms of post-war politics?
questions.correctAnswer: The Inspector represents post-war socialist values: collective responsibility, care for the vulnerable, equality. His final speech advocates the social solidarity that led to the welfare state. He is the voice of the new Britain Priestley wants.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response 30 marks: How does Priestley use the historical and social context of 1912 and 1945 to shape meaning in "An Inspector Calls"? <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Priestley exploits the gap between 1912 and 1945 as his most powerful dramatic device. By setting the play in the complacent pre-war era but writing for a post-war audience, he transforms every confident pronouncement Birling makes into a devastating irony. When Birling dismisses the possibility of war — "there isn't a chance of war" — and declares the Titanic "unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable," the 1945 audience recognises immediately that his capitalist certainties are hollow. This dramatic irony is not merely comic; it is Priestley's central argument that the individualist, hierarchical attitudes of 1912 led directly to global catastrophe. The social context of 1912 further sharpens Priestley's critique. Eva Smith's exploitation — sacked for asking for "twenty-five shillings a week" — reflects the absence of welfare provision, employment rights, or collective bargaining. Mrs Birling's refusal of charity to a "girl of that sort" exposes how voluntary welfare was subject to class prejudice. Priestley's 1945 audience, living alongside the new NHS and social security system, would recognise the Inspector's demand that "we are members of one body" as the philosophical foundation of the welfare state they had just created. Gender context is equally critical. Eva's powerlessness — pregnant, destitute, refused help by a women's committee led by the very class that oppresses her — shows how patriarchal and class systems intersect.
